blocks.content: Every collection stores its elements a little differently. An array keeps them in contiguous slots. A linked list chains them through pointers. A tree nests them in a branching structure.

If client code has to know which of these it is dealing with just to walk through the elements one by one, that client code becomes fragile. It breaks the moment the collection changes shape internally.

The Iterator pattern solves exactly this. It gives every collection a uniform way to be walked through, one element at a time, while keeping the internal layout completely hidden from whoever is doing the walking.

This is one of the most quietly used patterns in software. Almost every language bakes it into its core loop syntax, which is why it can feel invisible until you look closely at what a for-of loop or a for-each loop is actually doing under the hood.
Iterator provides a way to access the elements of a collection sequentially, without exposing the underlying representation of that collection.

The word sequentially is doing a lot of work in that definition. The iterator does not need to understand the whole collection at once. It only needs to know two things: is there a next element, and what is it.
1. The Problem: Every Collection Traverses Differently
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Every Collection Traverses Differently

blocks.content: Say a codebase has three kinds of collections in play: a plain array of tasks, a linked list of chat messages, and a tree of file system folders.
Each one needs a different piece of logic to walk through its elements in order.

["An array needs an integer index that increments from zero to length minus one.","A linked list needs a pointer that follows the next reference until it hits null.","A tree needs a traversal strategy, such as in-order, that uses recursion or an explicit stack."]
items: An array needs an integer index that increments from zero to length minus one.
A linked list needs a pointer that follows the next reference until it hits null.
A tree needs a traversal strategy, such as in-order, that uses recursion or an explicit stack.

blocks.content: The Naive Approach
Without an iterator, client code ends up branching on the type of collection it received, and then reaching into that collection to pull out its raw internals.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499534123-10207999.png
blocks.alt: Client code branching on collection type into separate array index, linked list pointer, and tree recursion traversal logic

blocks.content: This function now has to understand three different data structures. Add a fourth collection type, say a hash set, and this function needs another branch.
Why This Breaks Down

["Client code is coupled to internal fields like items, head, and next, so changing those fields breaks every caller.","Every new collection type means touching every place that loops over collections, instead of touching one place.","There is no shared contract, so two developers writing traversal logic for the same kind of collection can easily do it two different ways.","Encapsulation is broken. The whole point of a collection class is to hide how it stores data, and this approach throws that away."]
items: Client code is coupled to internal fields like items, head, and next, so changing those fields breaks every caller.
Every new collection type means touching every place that loops over collections, instead of touching one place.
There is no shared contract, so two developers writing traversal logic for the same kind of collection can easily do it two different ways.
Encapsulation is broken. The whole point of a collection class is to hide how it stores data, and this approach throws that away.

blocks.content: What is actually needed is a single, small contract that any collection can implement, and that any client code can rely on, regardless of what sits underneath.
2. Understanding the Iterator Pattern
The Iterator pattern introduces a small object, the iterator, whose only job is to remember where it currently is in a traversal and know how to move forward.
The collection itself does not do the walking. It just knows how to hand out an iterator when asked.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499536029-111942430.png
blocks.alt: Collection produces an iterator through createIterator, and client code talks only to that iterator through hasNext and next

blocks.content: The Two Roles

["Iterable, sometimes called Aggregate: the collection. Its job is to produce an iterator on request, through a method commonly called createIterator or iterator.","Iterator: the object that actually walks the collection. Its job is to answer two questions: is there more, and give me the next one."]
items: Iterable, sometimes called Aggregate: the collection. Its job is to produce an iterator on request, through a method commonly called createIterator or iterator.
Iterator: the object that actually walks the collection. Its job is to answer two questions: is there more, and give me the next one.

blocks.title: Two Separate Objects
blocks.content: The collection and the iterator are not the same object. A collection can even hand out several independent iterators at once, each remembering its own position, so two loops over the same list never interfere with each other.

This separation is the entire trick. The collection is free to store its data however it wants. The iterator is the only thing that needs to understand that storage, and it hides that understanding behind two tiny methods.
Internal Versus External Iterators
The style described here, where the client explicitly calls hasNext and next, is called an external iterator. The client drives the loop.

Some languages also support internal iterators, where the collection itself drives the loop and simply calls a function passed to it for every element, such as forEach. Both styles rely on the same underlying idea of hiding the traversal logic.
3. The hasNext and next Interface
Almost every iterator, in almost every language, boils down to the same two operations, even when the method names differ.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499537579-204885622.png
blocks.alt: Loop flow of calling hasNext to check for more elements, calling next and processing the element, then repeating until hasNext is false

blocks.content: hasNext
Answers a simple yes or no question: are there any elements left to visit? Client code calls this before every step so it knows when to stop.
next
Returns the next element in the sequence and moves the internal cursor forward by one step. Calling it again later returns whatever comes after that.

{"headers":["Concept","Java","JavaScript","Python"],"rows":[["Has more elements","hasNext returns boolean","done flag on the result object","raises StopIteration when exhausted"],["Get next element","next returns the element","next returns an object with value and done","__next__ returns the element"],["Get an iterator from a collection","iterator method from Iterable","Symbol.iterator method","__iter__ method"]]}
The names differ, but the shape is identical everywhere: a way to check for more, and a way to advance and read.

blocks.title: A Minimal Iterator Contract
blocks.text: interface Iterator has two methods: hasNext, which returns true or false, and next, which returns the next element and advances the cursor by one position. Any object that implements both can be looped over by any generic loop that only knows about this interface.

blocks.content: 4. Implementing a Custom Iterator From Scratch
blocks.text: 4. Implementing a Custom Iterator From Scratch

blocks.content: To make this concrete, consider a small custom collection called a Playlist, which stores songs internally in a plain array.
Nothing about the client code should need to know that an array is being used underneath. That is the whole point.
Step 1: Define the Iterator Contract
Both languages that support interfaces will define a small contract with hasNext and next.
Step 2: Implement a Concrete Iterator
The concrete iterator holds a reference to the collection and a cursor tracking the current position.
Step 3: Have the Collection Hand Out Iterators
blocks.text: Step 3: Have the Collection Hand Out Iterators

blocks.content: The Playlist class exposes a single method, createIterator, that returns a fresh PlaylistIterator every time it is called.
The internal field, songs, and the array holding it, never leave the Playlist and PlaylistIterator classes. Client code only ever sees hasNext and next.
5. Using the Custom Iterator in a Loop
blocks.text: 5. Using the Custom Iterator in a Loop

blocks.content: With the iterator in place, client code can walk the Playlist without ever touching the underlying array.

codes.python:
playlist = Playlist()
playlist.add_song('Song A')
playlist.add_song('Song B')
playlist.add_song('Song C')

it = playlist.create_iterator()
while it.has_next():
    song = it.next()
    print(song)

blocks.content: If the Playlist were rewritten tomorrow to store songs in a linked list instead of an array, none of this client code would need to change.
Only the internals of PlaylistIterator would need updating, because it is the only piece that ever touched the storage details.
Walking the Collection, Step by Step
blocks.text: Walking the Collection, Step by Step

blocks.content: The diagram below shows the shape of every one of these loops: the client only ever talks to the iterator, and the iterator is the only party that ever talks to the raw storage.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494831705-55688243.png
blocks.alt: Client code calling hasNext and next on an iterator, which internally walks an array, linked list, or tree, without the client seeing that internal structure

blocks.content: From the client side, an array, a linked list, and a tree are indistinguishable. Each one just answers hasNext and next.
6. How Built-in Language Constructs Use This Same Idea
blocks.text: 6. How Built-in Language Constructs Use This Same Idea

blocks.content: Most languages do not make developers write hasNext and next by hand for their own loops. They standardize the contract and wire a loop keyword directly into it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499539380-111467624.png
blocks.alt: JavaScript Symbol.iterator, Python dunder iter and dunder next, and Java Iterable and Iterator all implementing the same underlying iterator contract

blocks.content: JavaScript: the Iterable Protocol and for-of
blocks.text: JavaScript: the Iterable Protocol and for-of

blocks.content: An object becomes iterable in JavaScript by implementing a method named Symbol.iterator, which returns an iterator object with a next method.
That next method returns an object shaped like value and done, instead of using a separate hasNext call.
Python: __iter__, __next__, and StopIteration
Python asks an object for __iter__, which returns an iterator implementing __next__.
Instead of a boolean hasNext, Python simply raises a StopIteration exception from __next__ once there is nothing left, and the for loop catches that signal automatically.
Java: the Iterable and Iterator Interfaces
blocks.text: Java: the Iterable and Iterator Interfaces

blocks.content: Java standardizes this through two interfaces from java.util and java.lang: Iterable, with a single method iterator, and Iterator, with hasNext and next.
Any class implementing Iterable can be used directly inside a for-each loop, because the compiler quietly calls iterator, hasNext, and next behind the scenes.

Notice that the client loop looks identical across all three languages: for-of, for, and for-each. Each one is quietly running hasNext and next underneath, using whatever name the language gives those steps.
7. Worked Example: Iterating a Binary Search Tree
blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Iterating a Binary Search Tree

blocks.content: Arrays and linked lists are the easy cases. A tree is where the value of the Iterator pattern becomes obvious, because the traversal logic is genuinely more involved.
An in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes in ascending sorted order, but that traversal is naturally recursive. An iterator needs to expose it one step at a time instead.
The Trick: an Explicit Stack
A BST iterator keeps its own stack of nodes and pushes left children as it descends, which lets it pause between calls to next instead of running the whole recursion in one shot.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499541253-893995619.png
blocks.alt: Binary search tree iterator using an explicit stack to descend left children, then popping a node and pushing the left spine of its right child

blocks.content: The caller never sees a stack, a left pointer, or a right pointer. It only ever calls hasNext and next, the same two calls used for the array-backed Playlist earlier.
The Payoff

["The same client loop shape works whether the underlying collection is an array, a linked list, or a tree.","The traversal algorithm, however complex, is written once inside the iterator and never duplicated in client code.","Switching the traversal order, say to pre-order instead of in-order, only means swapping the iterator implementation."]
items: The same client loop shape works whether the underlying collection is an array, a linked list, or a tree.
The traversal algorithm, however complex, is written once inside the iterator and never duplicated in client code.
Switching the traversal order, say to pre-order instead of in-order, only means swapping the iterator implementation.

blocks.text: 8. Comparing This to Exposing Internals Directly

blocks.content: It helps to lay the two approaches side by side, since the tradeoff is not purely theoretical.

9. When a Custom Iterator Is Worth Writing
blocks.text: 9. When a Custom Iterator Is Worth Writing

blocks.content: Not every collection needs a hand written iterator. Most languages already give arrays, lists, and maps a built-in one for free.
Reach for a Built-in Collection When
blocks.text: Reach for a Built-in Collection When

blocks.content: ["The data really is just a list, set, or map, and a standard library type already models it well.","There is no custom traversal order or filtering logic layered on top of the raw storage.","Performance work has not identified the built-in type as a bottleneck."]
items: The data really is just a list, set, or map, and a standard library type already models it well.
There is no custom traversal order or filtering logic layered on top of the raw storage.
Performance work has not identified the built-in type as a bottleneck.

blocks.content: Write a Custom Iterator When

["The underlying structure is not a flat list, such as a tree, graph, or paginated remote data source.","The traversal needs to hide something meaningful, like lazily fetching the next page from a network call only when next is invoked.","Multiple traversal orders need to exist side by side, such as in-order and pre-order over the same tree, without duplicating client code.","The collection is part of a public API, where hiding the storage choice protects consumers from future internal changes."]
items: The underlying structure is not a flat list, such as a tree, graph, or paginated remote data source.
The traversal needs to hide something meaningful, like lazily fetching the next page from a network call only when next is invoked.
Multiple traversal orders need to exist side by side, such as in-order and pre-order over the same tree, without duplicating client code.
The collection is part of a public API, where hiding the storage choice protects consumers from future internal changes.

blocks.title: A Practical Rule of Thumb
blocks.content: If a piece of code loops over the same custom structure in more than one place, and that loop keeps repeating the same walk-the-pointers logic, that repetition is the signal to pull it out into an iterator.

The underlying question is always the same one this pattern was built to answer: should the code that consumes a collection know how that collection is built. Usually, the answer is no, and an iterator is the cleanest way to keep it that way.
